newsitem.title: USA: Motion Picture's Valenti opposes changing ratings.
newsitem.headline: Motion Picture's Valenti opposes changing ratings.

text.p: LAS VEGAS (Rueter) - Motion Picture Association of America Chairman Jack Valenti, who led the effort to fashion new television ratings, said Monday he would oppose revising the system so soon after it was put into place.

Parents should be given time to get accustomed to the ratings and the ratings should be allowed to be used in conjunction with the "V-chip" device before any tinkering is done with them, Valenti said at the annual National Association of Broadcaster's convention.
Valenti said he would not make any revisions "until and unless real parents and real kids tell us they want changes to be made."
Some critics of the system have suggested changes to three single-letter designations: S for sexual content, L for objectional language and V for violence.
Valenti said those letter designations would only confuse parents trying to monitor TV programs watched by their children.

For example CBS TV's "Touched by an Angel" which is highly regarded by family groups, might require S and V designations since there are scenes showing people hugging and kissing and storylines that feature angels defeating evil forces, Valenti said.
Yet movies shown on TV, such as "Natural Born Killers," would also carry the same designation.
"Without advanced information, how can they gauge the intensity of the S, the L and the V?" he said.

Suggestions that the lettered ratings could also offer numerical suffixes to provide a glimpse into the degree of sexual, violent or language content would only complicate the ratings, he said. A convoluted rating system would lead to a bulky and unwieldy remote control with the "V-chip" device.
Sounding a familiar theme among broadcasters at this year's convention, Valenti urged politicians in Washington to avoid meddling with the system.
Parents should be the soul arbiters of the value of the current ratings, particularly since they were imposed just three months ago.
"Congress has no authority to lessen the reach of the First Amendment - not now, not tomorrow, not ever," he said.
